problem: The equation is written σ = Ft / (Cv b mn y) with y called the Lewis form factor read for zv. With the standard Indian textbook tooth form factor y (values around 0.1, e.g. y = 0.154 − 0.912/zv ≈ 0.11 for zv = 22), the π factor is missing. As printed, the calculated bending stress comes out about 3.14 times too small, so a tooth that is actually overstressed passes as safe — an unsafe design.
fix: Write the equation with the definition of y made explicit: σ = Ft / (Cv b π mn y), where y is the tooth form factor from the standard table (about 0.1) read for zv. If your table instead lists Y = πy (values around 0.3–0.4), use σ = Ft / (Cv b mn Y). Never mix a table of y with the form of the equation that expects Y.

where: Section 2, first sentence of the virtual teeth part
problem: 'The normal section of a helical tooth is an ellipse' is loose: it is the intersection of the normal plane with the pitch cylinder that is an ellipse, not the tooth section itself. A student may picture the tooth cross-section as an ellipse.
fix: The normal plane cuts the pitch cylinder in an ellipse, not a true circle, so the tooth curvature in that plane is larger than the pitch radius.

problem: 'each bearing must take its gear's thrust' suggests both bearings of a shaft carry thrust. In normal practice one bearing is located to take the thrust and the other is free to float axially.
fix: The thrusts on the two gears are equal and opposite along the shaft, so each shaft needs a locating bearing (angular contact or tapered roller) to take its own thrust; the other bearing is left free to float.
